lesson.title: ge- ↔ y-: the Ancient Participle
lesson.subtitle: Participle formation drills — and the yclept/genug etymology box

hook.title: The Prefix That Survived in One Word
hook.content: Weak-verb participles are pure assembly: ge- + stem + -t. gesagt. gelernt. gemacht. The formula is so regular it is boring — which is why the etymology is worth the whole lesson: that ge- is the prefix English wore down to y- and then dropped. Yclept ('called'), ywis ('surely'), ybounden — Chaucer's participles are German participles with a y. And one ge- word escaped the purge entirely — enough, whose initial e- IS the old ge-, standing today inside genug's twin. Say genug and you are pronouncing Chaucer's grammar.

footnotes.title: The One-Word Museum
footnotes.content: genug ← OE ġenōg ← Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz: ge- + *nōgaz 'to reach, attain'. 'Enough' reached the same word through the same route. It is the only everyday English word where the ancient participial prefix survives in place — a one-word museum of the entire system.

pattern.title: The Weak-Participle Assembly Line
pattern.content: Feed a regular verb into the line: stem + ge- in front + -t at the back. lernen → gelernt, sagen → gesagt, machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft. Vowel? Untouched — that is what makes it weak (regular). Motion verbs ride sein instead of haben and keep the same participle: wandern → (ist) gewandert. The -ieren and ver- verbs keep skipping ge-: studiert, verstanden. And genug is your mnemonic anchor: every ge- you stamp from now on is the same ancient prefix that enough smuggled into English.
pattern.linguist_note: The ge- zone: only verbs with FIRST-syllable stress take it. Words whose stress moved (ver-, be-, er- verbs; -ieren verbs) reject ge- — the acoustic law from the No-ge- Club now explains the whole map.

exercises.prompt: Assembly line: build the participle of 'lernen':
exercises.explanation: ge- + stem + -t: gelernt. Weak participles never touch the vowel.

exercises.prompt: Which everyday English word still carries the ancient ge- prefix?
options: enough (the e- is the old y-/ge-)
exercises.target_answer: enough (the e- is the old y-/ge-)
exercises.explanation: OE ġenōg → enough: the unstressed y- reduced to e-. Genug is the same word, prefix intact. The weekend file uses the same bracket: Am Wochenende habe ich alles gebucht — buchen (book) took its beech-wood name before it took your reservation.

exercises.prompt: Match each infinitive with its participle (the last one breaks the -t pattern — a preview):
exercises.explanation: ge- + stem + -t for the first four — even the motion verb gewandert, which just switches its auxiliary to sein. getragen sneaks in -en instead of -t: the strong verbs are coming (next lesson).

exercises.prompt: Which auxiliary does 'wandern' take in the Perfekt?
options: sein — motion verbs ride sein: Wir sind gewandert
exercises.target_answer: sein — motion verbs ride sein: Wir sind gewandert
exercises.explanation: Going somewhere under your own power → sein. Wandern is the textbook case: Wir sind gestern gewandert. Ankommen rides sein too — arrival is motion's finish line.
sein opens the bracket for motion, gewandert closes it: 'Wir sind gestern gewandert'.
cues: Start with "Wir" and anchor "sind" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Assemble weak participles at speed and pick haben vs sein by motion.
summary.takeaway: ge- + stem + -t builds the weak participle — the same ge- that English kept only inside enough.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: haben or sein? — the choice gym where motion decides the auxiliary.

genug.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz with the ancient ge- prefix — the same prefix English wore down to y- (yclept, ywis) and buried inside 'enough'. [wiktionary]

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

kaufen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, borrowed from Latin caupō 'tradesman/innkeeper' — the same loan that gave English cheap; collateral cognates. [wiktionary]

tragen.etymology_derivation: Class 6 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *draganą (to carry, drag) - the twin of English draw and drag; tragen-trug-getragen matches draw-drew-drawn. [wiktionary]

ankommen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anakwemana, to come to — an + kommen, with archaic English oncome as the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

buchen.context_translation: I am booking a hotel online.
buchen.etymology_derivation: From Buch plus -en (the beechwood-carving word); the modern reserve sense was modelled after English to book — a semantic loan the page documents. [wiktionary]

wochenende.context_phrase: Am Wochenende fahren wir an den See.
wochenende.context_translation: On the weekend we go to the lake.
wochenende.etymology_derivation: Woche + Ende — the modern compound arose in the 19th century as a calque of English weekend; Woche is the twin of week (k → ch) and Ende the twin of end. [wiktionary]

sommer.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sumar — English summer is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

winter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wintruz — English winter is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

sandale.etymology_derivation: A 16th-century borrowing of Latin sandalium, from Greek sandalon, from Old Persian - the same Greek word that gave English sandal. [wiktionary][etymonline]

beide.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bai, the ancient Germanic dual meaning both, two; the same root grew into English both, which fused it with a demonstrative. [wiktionary]

kunde.context_phrase: Der Kunde wartet an der Kasse.
kunde.context_translation: The customer is waiting at the checkout.
kunde.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *kuntho, a known one — the page lists Old English cutha as cognate, the uncouth family: a customer is one you know. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
